segments.text: Five ways the Central Limit Theorem runs the real world.
segments.caption: 5 ways the Central Limit Theorem runs the real world.

segments.text: Election polls, A-B tests, factories, insurance, and machine learning. Save this one!
segments.caption: Election polls, A/B tests, factories, insurance, and machine learning. Save this one!

segments.text: Quick recap. Take many samples and average each one.
segments.caption: Quick recap. Take many samples and average each one.

segments.text: Even if the data is skewed, those averages form a bell curve.
segments.caption: Even if the data is skewed, those averages form a bell curve.

segments.text: And their spread, the standard error, is sigma over root n. More data, a narrower bell.
segments.caption: And their spread, the standard error, is sigma over root n. More data, a narrower bell.

segments.text: Use one: election polls.
segments.caption: Use one: election polls.

segments.text: A pollster asks one thousand voters out of millions. Each answer is just yes or no, nowhere near a bell curve.
segments.caption: A pollster asks 1,000 voters out of millions. Each answer is just yes or no, nowhere near a bell curve.

segments.text: But the share saying yes is an average, so it's roughly normal. That's why fifty-two percent, plus or minus three, is a real ninety-five percent range.
segments.caption: But the share saying yes is an average, so it's roughly normal. That's why 52% ±3% is a real 95% range.

segments.text: And to halve that margin, you need four times the people: four thousand voters gives plus or minus one and a half.
segments.caption: And to halve that margin, you need 4 times the people: 4,000 voters gives ±1.5%.

segments.text: Use two: A-B tests.
segments.caption: Use two: A/B tests.

segments.text: Customer spending is very skewed: most people spend a little, and a few spend a lot.
segments.caption: Customer spending is very skewed: most people spend a little, and a few spend a lot.

segments.text: But the average spend over thousands of users is normal. That's why a simple z or t test can compare version A with version B.
segments.caption: But the average spend over thousands of users is normal. That's why a simple z or t test can compare version A with version B.

segments.text: Use three: factories.
segments.caption: Use three: factories.

segments.text: Every hour, a juice plant weighs five bottles and plots their average on a control chart.
segments.caption: Every hour, a juice plant weighs 5 bottles and plots their average on a control chart.

segments.text: The averages stay within three standard errors, ninety-nine point seven percent of the time. A point outside the lines means: stop the machine.
segments.caption: The averages stay within 3 standard errors, 99.7% of the time. A point outside the lines means: stop the machine.

segments.text: Use four: insurance.
segments.caption: Use four: insurance.

segments.text: One customer's claims are unpredictable: nothing for years, then one huge claim.
segments.caption: One customer's claims are unpredictable: nothing for years, then one huge claim.

segments.text: But across a hundred thousand customers, the average claim is very predictable. Its standard error shrinks about three hundred times. That's how premiums are set.
segments.caption: But across 100,000 customers, the average claim is very predictable. Its standard error shrinks about 300 times. That's how premiums are set.

segments.text: Use five: machine learning.
segments.caption: Use five: machine learning.

segments.text: A model scores ninety percent accuracy on one thousand test examples. Each prediction is just right or wrong.
segments.caption: A model scores 90% accuracy on 1,000 test examples. Each prediction is just right or wrong.

segments.text: But accuracy is an average, so it's roughly normal, with a standard error of about one percent. The true accuracy is about eighty-eight to ninety-two percent.
segments.caption: But accuracy is an average, so it's roughly normal, with a standard error of about 1%. The true accuracy is about 88 to 92%.

segments.text: Test on ten thousand examples, and the range tightens to about plus or minus point six.
segments.caption: Test on 10,000 examples, and the range tightens to about ±0.6%.

segments.text: See the pattern? The raw data is messy, but averages behave. That's why the bell curve shows up everywhere.
segments.caption: See the pattern? The raw data is messy, but averages behave. That's why the bell curve shows up everywhere.

segments.text: In fact, every z-test, t-test, and confidence interval on this page leans on this one theorem.
segments.caption: In fact, every z-test, t-test, and confidence interval on this page leans on this one theorem.

segments.text: Two interview traps.
segments.caption: Two interview traps.

segments.text: One: the theorem is about averages, not the data. Individual values stay skewed.
segments.caption: One: the theorem is about averages, not the data. Individual values stay skewed.

segments.text: Two: it needs independent samples and enough data: about thirty for mild skew, far more for heavy tails like incomes.
segments.caption: Two: it needs independent samples and enough data: about 30 for mild skew, far more for heavy tails like incomes.
